deep_dives.title: Figure melts its retired F.02 humanoid robots by having them leap into molten steel

facts.fact: Figure posted the film 'F02 decommission' on September 30, 2026; it runs 3 minutes 40 seconds and CEO Brett Adcock says the video is real.
The F.02 robots were sent to a foundry in Imatra, Finland, and leaped autonomously into a 75-ton electric arc furnace.
Arnold Schwarzenegger told Figure to 'melt them' and later joined the project.
Figure says the footage was not digitally generated; the robots physically travelled to Finland and performed the jumps themselves.
A new AI control model was trained in simulation using stunt performers' movements as reference; Figure also practised with airbags, having robots leap from a second floor at its San Jose HQ.
The team had 24 hours and six melts; each melt allowed only a ~20-minute window before the steel crusted over.
Figure had even sought help from former MythBusters members while looking for a facility willing to accept the robots.
The recovered metal is being machined into a limited run of commemorative F.02 artifacts; protected components were destroyed so no one could reuse them.

deep_dives.title: Crew-13 makes fastest-ever US spacecraft trip to the ISS: 7 h 55 min

facts.fact: Crew-13 launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 / Dragon on Thursday Oct 1, 2026 at 11:10 a.m. EDT from Space Launch Complex 40, Cape Canaveral.
Dragon docked at 7:05 p.m. EDT on Oct 1, 7 hours 55 minutes after launch: the fastest any American spacecraft has reached the ISS.
Previous US record was 12 h 33 min (cargo Dragon CRS-31, Nov 2024); fastest crewed US trip before was 14 h 43 min (Crew-11, Aug 2025).
Overall crewed record remains Russia's Soyuz MS-17: 3 h 3 min on Oct 14, 2020.
Crew: NASA's Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, CSA's Joshua Kutryk, Roscosmos' Sergey Teteryatnikov.
Dragon docked to the forward-facing port of the Harmony module.
Watkins is the first NASA astronaut to launch on Dragon twice (previously Crew-4, 170 days in space in 2022).
Kutryk is the first Canadian launched under NASA's Commercial Crew Program, on a ~6-month mission, carrying a 100+-year-old family pocket watch.
Launch had slipped from Sept 30 to Oct 1.

deep_dives.title: Google's Project Suncatcher puts its first AI chips (TPUs) into orbit

facts.fact: SpaceX launched Transporter-18 from Vandenberg at 11:22 a.m. PT on Oct 1, 2026 with 130 payloads to sun-synchronous orbit.
The Suncatcher prototype is one satellite built with Planet carrying four Google TPUs (Trillium generation); it is the first in-orbit test of Project Suncatcher.
Solar panels supply about 1 kW; the chips run short Gemini/AI inference workloads in ~15-minute windows before shutting down to cool.
Google first announced Project Suncatcher as a research moonshot in November 2025.
The long-term design envisions clusters of 81 satellites within a 1 km radius at ~650 km altitude, linked by free-space lasers.
Planet is contracted for two more prototype satellites targeting 2027 to test high-bandwidth laser links; the satellite uses the bus of Planet's next-gen Owl satellite.
Same rideshare also carried Planet's Tanager-2 (with Carbon Mapper) and 18 SuperDoves.

deep_dives.title: India's TakeMe2Space launches MOI-1A, billed as India's first orbital computing satellite

facts.fact: MOI-1A was manifested on SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare, which launched at 11:22 a.m. PT on Oct 1, 2026 (some Indian outlets had cited Oct 2 as the date).
TakeMe2Space calls MOI-1A India's first orbital computing satellite.
It weighs about 14 kg in a 6U CubeSat configuration.
It uses Nvidia Orin NX edge processors (up to 117 TOPS) and about 150 W of power to run customer AI models in orbit.
It processes Earth-observation imagery on board and downlinks only the results, cutting raw data transfer.
23 customers, including mapping firms and universities, have signed up.
Its predecessor MOI-1 was lost in January 2026 after an anomaly on ISRO's PSLV-C62 mission.
CAVEAT: as of research time no source confirmed MOI-1A is operating in orbit; say 'launched', not 'working'.

deep_dives.title: OpenAI launches Dots: always-on ChatGPT agents with their own cloud computers

facts.fact: OpenAI launched dots on Tuesday, Sept 29, 2026 at DevDay 2026 in San Francisco.
Each dot runs on GPT-6 Astra (introduced Sept 3) and works from its own cloud computer and browser.
Dots connect to more than 4,000 apps via plugins and keep working on goals in the background without re-prompting.
Users set Custom Rules for what a dot may do alone, must ask about, or must never do; linking a personal computer is optional and off by default.
Rolling out to ChatGPT Pro and Business Premium; first dot included with Pro 100/200/500 ($100/$200/$500 per month).
Pro access excludes the EEA, Switzerland and the UK for now.
Alongside dots OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Sol at $2/$10 per million input/output tokens, one-fifth of Astra's price.
